title: Battery health of used EVs varies significantly - electrive.com
content:
Automobile
While the battery health of used EVs has an undeserved reputation, an evaluation of over 500,000 battery tests by Aviloo demonstrates that the capacity loss of used traction batteries varies widely. A manufacturer-independent battery test should therefore precede any purchase decision.
Aviloo Box for measuring battery health
Image: Aviloo
First, it’s important to note that the Austrian startup Aviloo generates its revenue by using its proprietary Aviloo Flash Test to determine the State of Health (SoH) of electric vehicle batteries. The company collaborates with car dealerships, professional used car dealers, and leasing companies, which conduct these tests via the OBD interface of the EVs. The result is a manufacturer-independent State of Health for each vehicle – and this is particularly relevant for used cars.
According to Aviloo, vehicles’ built-in battery condition displays are often unreliable. While buyers of internal combustion engine cars primarily focus on age and mileage, the condition of the traction battery is especially critical for electric vehicles. This is because every EV is affected by
degradation
; an ageing process that leads to a permanent loss of storage capacity and, consequently, range. Most manufacturers today guarantee that an EV will retain at least 70 per cent of its original battery capacity after eight years or 160,000 km. This sets a benchmark against which used electric vehicles must be measured.
More than 500,000 EVs tested for battery health
With this in mind: for its new ‘Aviloo Certified EV Battery Report’, which will be published semi-annually in the future, Aviloo has analysed data from over 500,000 used EVs. These were tested using the independent Aviloo Flash Test worldwide, so that different climate zones could also be accounted for. The analysis focused on 20 particularly common EV models, for which the report specifies the median battery condition at three mileage levels: 50,000 km, 100,000 km, and 150,000 km.
Comparing the three mileage levels reveals three clear patterns, as Aviloo states: First, the median battery health decreases with increasing mileage – which is hardly surprising, as wear and tear naturally increases with distance travelled. Second, the differences between individual vehicles grow with mileage; degradation is real and increases with the distance covered. Equally important is the third pattern: the differences between models remain consistent across all three mileage levels.
Looking at the model ranking, 16 out of the 20 EV models examined still have a median State of Health of at least 90 per cent after 150,000 km, while the remaining four models fall within the 85 to 90 per cent range. This means that all 20 models, even at the typical warranty limit of 160,000 km, still have a median State of Health well above the warranty-relevant 70 per cent – specifically between 80 and 90 per cent.
However, it is important to note that the average obscures the fact that there are significant outliers – both high and low – for every model analysed. For example, the Aviloo database shows that the Hyundai Ioniq 5 (72.6 kWh) has an average SoH of 92.8 per cent after 150,000 km, corresponding to a range of around 319 km. Yet, the spread between individual vehicles of this model at 150,000 km mileage is over 12 per cent SoH, which translates to a range difference of around 42 km.
Marcus Berger, CEO of AVILOO, says: “The truth in this data is that averages hide a lot. Yes, EV batteries are ageing better than the ‘they wear out fast’ myth suggests – but that’s not the most useful thing this report tells you. What matters is that battery health varies significantly between models, and even more between individual cars of the same model. A gap of ten or fifteen percent in state of health is a real difference in range, in what a car is worth, and in what you can rely on it for. You simply can’t know where your car sits in that range without testing it independently.”
Berger’s recommendation is therefore clear: he believes that anyone buying a used EV should have an Aviloo Flash Test performed beforehand to determine the battery health—that is, the actual remaining capacity of the battery.

title: 'SHERLOCK' project aims to standardise black mass for battery recycling - electrive.com
content:
A new German research project is developing standardised quality classes for black mass, a key intermediate product in the recycling of lithium-ion batteries, with the aim of making battery recycling more efficient.
The SHERLOCK project aims to develop uniform quality classes for black mass.
Image: Fraunhofer ISC
During the recycling of lithium-ion batteries, mechanical processing produces what is known as black mass. This fine-grained material contains valuable battery raw materials such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, and
graphite
, which can be recovered in subsequent processing steps. However, black mass is far from uniform: its composition depends on factors such as the battery’s cell chemistry, age and usage of the battery, as well as the specific recycling process.
These differences can complicate further processing. Impurities can reduce the efficiency of downstream recycling processes and compromise the quality of the recovered recyclates. This is where the newly launched SHERLOCK research project comes in. It aims to develop methods for precisely and reproducibly determining the composition and quality of different black mass materials.
Standardised quality classes for black mass
A central objective of the project is the development of standardised quality classes for black mass. To this end, the project will examine material from industrial recycling processes alongside specifically produced model materials, allowing researchers to investigate how certain impurities can affect direct and hydrometallurgical recycling methods. The results will be used to create a criteria catalogue that can be used to assess black mass and assign it to an appropriate recycling pathway. Researchers will also explore methods for removing impurities, as well as hybrid process chains that combine direct and hydrometallurgical recycling methods.
A variety of spectroscopic and magnetic analysis methods will be employed. Ensuring that different laboratories and recycling companies achieve comparable results is particularly important for future industrial applications. SHERLOCK will therefore develop uniform guidelines for sample preparation, calibration, and measurement conditions. The technical specifications will later be submitted to DIN and ISO standardisation committees.
Ultimately, stronger characterisation of the raw materials and contaminants in black mass could enable downstream recycling processes to be tailored more closely to the material being processed. This could reduce material losses and improve the quality of the recovered battery raw materials. However, the project must first demonstrate whether this can also measurably reduce recycling costs.
Battery recycling: viability remains an obstacle
However, economic viability remains one of the biggest challenges for battery recycling in Europe. A recent study published as part of the
EU Safeloop project
estimates current losses at around €1.90 euros per kg of battery pack. Key cost drivers include hazardous goods transport, dismantling, and uncertainties in material recovery. Better-characterised black mass and tailored recycling processes could address some of these losses.
At the same time, regulatory requirements are increasing. The EU Battery Regulation will soon mandate higher recovery rates for battery raw materials such as lithium, nickel, and cobalt. From August 2031, minimum proportions of recycled materials in new vehicle batteries will also apply. This will require not only sufficient recycling capacity but also reliably defined quality of the recovered materials.
The topic also plays a role in the CO
balance of electric cars. A recent
study by TU München
calls for greater regulatory recognition of savings achieved through battery recycling and a stronger circular economy for raw materials. Regardless, the EU Battery Regulation already sets concrete requirements for the circular use of battery raw materials. Standardised assessment of black mass could help close these material loops more efficiently.
The SHERLOCK project involves the MEET Battery Research Centre at the University of Münster, the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt, the Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung und -prüfung, the Fraunhofer Institute for Silicate Research, and the Öko-Institut, as well as Pure Devices and phase VISION. Partners from the recycling industry are also providing black mass from industrial processes for the investigations.

title: Q&A: Standardized Imaging Enhances Battery Research Reliability
content:
Lithium-Ion Batteries
EV Batteries
Design & Manufacturing
Materials
Interviews
Explore insights from Dr. Zhao Liu of Thermo Fisher Scientific on a standardized imaging framework improving battery research reliability and energy storage innovation.
September 2, 2026
6 Min Read
Researcher at the University of Chicago’s Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering.
Courtesy of UChicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering / John Zich.
Battery Technology
recently interviewed Dr. Zhao Liu, Senior Market Development Manager at Thermo Fisher Scientific, to discuss groundbreaking advancements in battery research. The conversation centered around new findings published in
, titled "
Guidelines for Correlative Imaging and Analysis of Reactive Alkali Metal Battery Materials
The study led by Professor Ying Shirley Meng and her team at the
University of Chicago’s Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering
and the Energy Storage Research Alliance (ESRA) at Argonne National Laboratory, in collaboration with
Thermo Fisher Scientific
highlights critical challenges in electron microscopy techniques used to study lithium and sodium battery materials. The research reveals that these techniques can cause significant damage to
battery materials
during sample transfer and imaging—more than previously recognized. The findings point toward a standardized framework that the battery research community can adopt to make results more reliable, reproducible, and comparable across labs.
Related:
Donut Lab Battery Breakdown Highlights Importance of Independent Testing
In this Q&A, Dr. Liu provides expert perspectives on the implications of these findings and the future of imaging technologies in advancing energy storage research.
In what specific ways does this framework contribute to the development of longer-lasting EV and grid-storage batteries?
Dr. Zhao Liu, Senior Market Development Manager at Thermo Fisher Scientific
A battery's lifecycle is determined at the nanoscale. The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) governs how efficiently lithium or sodium cycles, and its structure and chemistry decide if a cell holds capacity over the years of service an electric vehicle (EV) pack or a grid installation requires. Lithium and sodium metals are some of the most promising anode materials for next-gen batteries, but their sensitivity to air, moisture and the electron or ion beams that are used in characterization makes them difficult to capture their native structure. Without careful control of these factors, researchers risk mistaking imaging-induced artifacts for actual battery degradation.
Preserving the native structure and chemistry of these materials during sample preparation, transfer and imaging allows the framework to guide more accurate characterization of battery interfaces and degradation processes, which are critical in determining capacity fade, cycle life and safety. A deeper understanding of how these materials interact with one another gives researchers more reliable results for designing improved electrolytes, more stable SEIs and more durable electrode architectures.
Related:
How Europe Can Lead the Solid-State Battery Race
Our research also found that high-resolution imaging of pure lithium metal is possible at atomic resolution without cryogenic conditions if sample transfer is carefully controlled, while the more beam-sensitive SEI layers still require cryo-protections. That distinction lets labs reserve cryo workflows for the samples that need them.
For EV batteries, the framework can speed the development of high-energy lithium-metal batteries with enhanced cycle life and safety.
What challenges in battery research does this framework overcome, and how does it improve the reliability and reproducibility of results?
The framework addresses one of the biggest challenges in imaging battery materials with electron microscopy, which is preserving highly reactive materials in their native state throughout the characterization process. The study demonstrates that even with as little as 15 seconds of air exposure, conventional gallium focused ion beam (Ga⁺ FIB) preparation, cryogenic sample transfer, and uncontrolled electron beam exposure can each introduce artifacts that alter the true structure and chemistry of battery materials.
These artifacts are why different labs report different results for the same battery materials. Our literature review also found that many cryo-electron microscopy studies did not report critical imaging parameters, which could make it challenging to determine whether the observed structures reflect the actual material or beam-induced damage.
Related:
ProLogium CEO Shares Insights on Solid-State Battery Leadership
To improve the reliability and reproducibility of battery characterization, the framework establishes a standardized workflow that includes sample storage, inert sample transfer, focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) preparation, imaging temperature selection and electron dose control during transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis. It also provides guidelines for reporting key experimental parameters, including dose rate, imaging temperature and sample transfer conditions, to provide researchers with a common benchmark for comparing and reproducing results. The way labs handle samples determines reliability and how they report results impacts reproducibility. This framework provides a structure for standardization across these two key elements in battery research.
Correlative imaging workflow for TEM through different sample transfer methods to observe reactive lithium metal down to the atomic scale. Courtesy of Joule under CC-BY-NC.
How can battery research labs worldwide integrate this framework into their workflows, and what steps are needed for it to become a global standard?
Labs can easily adopt this framework by incorporating it into a standardized workflow that covers every stage of the characterization process. That means minimizing glovebox storage time, maintaining continuous inert-gas protection during sample transfer, selecting room-temperature or cryogenic imaging based on the specific material being studied, and carefully controlling electron dose throughout TEM analysis.
Core microscopy facilities can help establish the framework as a best practice rather than outlining laboratory-specific protocols. However, broader implementation will require collaboration across the battery research industry, including standardized reporting guidelines, reference materials, instrument-specific dose calibration, operator training, and interlaboratory benchmarking studies. To make this a true industry standard, journals, reviewers and funding programs should also look to include dose reporting in the same way they request other experimental parameters.
What role does atomic resolution imaging play in identifying and addressing issues with reactive alkali metals in battery materials?
Atomic-resolution TEM is one of the most promising ways that scientists can see the features that determine how materials interact with each other. In the development of next-gen batteries, critical processes such as lithium or sodium deposition and SEI evolution begin at the atomic scale. Without this level of resolution, it's challenging to determine why a battery degrades or how to improve it.
This resolution also makes results harder to interpret because it can introduce more components that could be interpreted as errors. At atomic resolution, the energy delivered by the beam is enough to transform the very features being studied, such as the lithium fluoride decomposition. Atomic-resolution imaging plays a dual role in this framework. It helps scientists better understand reactive alkali metals, but it also demands the most rigorous control. If the transfer history and beam dose are not documented, a beam-induced change can look like a new discovery. The framework makes EM tools as trustworthy as it is powerful.
How do you see this framework influencing the future of battery innovation and the adoption of next-generation energy storage technologies?
Battery innovation isn't held back by a lack of ideas so much as by how hard it is to build on other researchers' results. A standardized characterization framework lets findings travel between labs, so even a poor result becomes useful information rather than a dead end. For every lab that adopts the practice, the design-test-learn loop that carries a chemistry from the lab to a cell ready for validation gets shorter. This approach reduces experimental complexity while improving data quality and confidence in the results.
Battery researchers are also investigating different or novel materials that are proving to be more challenging to study. As the field moves toward sodium-ion for cost-sensitive applications and toward other next-generation chemistries, the compounds involved become progressively more air- and beam-sensitive, which raises the bar for proper characterization as commercial stakes grow. Establishing these workflows and disclosure standards now, before those chemistries mature into production, means the foundational data underneath these chemistries will be consistent from the start. Looking ahead, a standardized correlative imaging workflow will enable more consistent and comparable results across universities, national laboratories and industry.

title: AI Drives Shift in Stationary Battery Applications | Battery Tech
content:
Stationary Batteries
Design & Manufacturing
Battery Management Systems
Market Analysis
Interviews
Hyperscale computing facilities are moving from traditional backup power to high-rate, dynamic load management—creating specifications that favor energy density, cycle life, and power delivery over cost alone.
September 2, 2026
7 Min Read
The Stargate Oracle AI data center campus on August 26, 2026 in Abilene, Texas. The Stargate Oracle AI data center will span roughly 4 million square feet and will be operated by Oracle for OpenAI.
Brandon Bell/Getty Images
At a Glance
Beyond backup, batteries buffer dynamic loads in real time, balancing AI computing, grid power, and on-site renewables.
Moving battery storage closer to computing loads simplifies power architecture and eliminates redundant conversion stages.
Advanced cells smooth millisecond power spikes, deliver fast ride-through, and support high-voltage DC at megawatt scale.
As AI data centers scale past 100 GW of global capacity, the humble backup battery is undergoing its most dramatic transformation in 50 years.
For most of the modern data center's history, critical power was a solved problem, and the solution was lead-acid. Valve-regulated lead-acid strings sat in a dedicated battery room behind a double-conversion UPS, and the job description was one sentence long: hold the load for the ten to thirty seconds it takes a diesel generator to start and accept load.
Nothing about that duty cycle rewarded innovation. Racks drew 3 to 15 kW. Loads were diverse, aggregated, and statistically smooth as a floor full of enterprise IT and general cloud VMs does not move in unison.
The battery was insurance, specified on minutes of runtime and purchased on price. Lead-acid's low cost, mature supply chain, and predictable failure behavior made it very hard to displace.
Lithium-ion finally started to displace it over the past decade, and the argument was mostly logistical: a third of the footprint, longer service life, better monitoring, lower total cost across a refresh cycle. However the mandate did not change and the battery still bridged to the generator.
Related:
NeoVolta, SK On Announce One of Largest Domestic Battery Deals Since OBBBA Passage
AI has changed the mandate. Not because AI data centers need more backup, but because they need something backup was never designed to provide: a power buffer that responds to the load rather than to the utility.
Current state of AI data center battery technology
AI rack power density: From 15 kW to 1 MW+
The AI rack is where this becomes concrete. Traditional facilities ran 3 to 15 kW per rack; AI clusters now run 40 to 140+ kW, with hyperscale campuses scaled from 100 MW into the multi-gigawatt range for training.
Global installed data center capacity passed 100 GW in early 2025, and interconnection queues of two to eleven years have pushed hyperscalers toward proprietary campuses with on-site generation and storage.
Three-tier battery architecture emerges
At roughly 100 kW per rack the distribution architecture is still 415 V AC. But the storage stack has already split into three tiers.
Facility-scale BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) sits at the grid interface for peak shaving, frequency regulation, and renewables integration. The UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) layer provides short-duration ride-through until generators take over.
And battery backup units have migrated into the rack itself where OCP's (Open Compute Project) ORv3 design puts a 48 V battery shelf alongside the 48 V power shelf, inches from the accelerators, cutting conversion losses and absorbing variable load without a heavy centralized UPS footprint.
Related:
Cummins Wins Its Largest BESS Contract for US Data Center Project
Power vs. energy: The new specification challenge
That third tier exists because of the load profile. Training campuses tolerate brief interruptions but throw 40 to 60% swings when large jobs start and pause, the "warble" that operators now design around.
Inference campuses tolerate nothing: five-nines uptime (99.999%), sub-50 ms cutover, sustained two- to four-hour cover for always-on fleets. These are not the same specification, and neither is satisfied by cheap energy.
Credit: Volta Foundation Battery Report 2025
Requirements now span five orders of magnitude in duration, and no single chemistry covers them. What the rack-level bands share is that they are power problems, not energy problems.
The cell is being asked for high current for a short time, tens of thousands of times, in a hot and space-constrained enclosure, with a failure mode that must never propagate.
But today's 100 kW racks are just the beginning. The next generation will force a complete architectural rethink.
The 800V DC revolution: Future of data center battery systems
The breaking point: Why 415V AC can't scale
The next rack generation is where the architecture breaks and reforms. Racks are heading toward and past 1 MW, with individual accelerators projected in the 5 kW range.
Related:
7 Residential Battery Storage Systems Worth Buying in 2026
At that density, 415 V AC distribution stops working: copper, conversion losses, and the physical volume of AC infrastructure all become binding constraints.
High-voltage DC architecture takes center stage
The industry answer, developed through the Open Compute Project and pushed hard by NVIDIA, is 800 V DC from a medium-voltage rectifier or solid-state transformer (SST) straight to the rack.
The published roadmap moves in stages: an HVDC (High-Voltage DC) sidecar alongside compute racks near term, an HVDC rack in facility grey space after that, and eventually an outdoor SST feeding IT racks directly at 1 MW+. Each stage removes conversion.
That matters arithmetically: even at 99% efficiency, one conversion stage in a gigawatt facility burns roughly 10 MW, equivalent to the draw of about seventy high-density racks.
Credit: Digitimes via PRNewswire
Battery technology requirements in HVDC systems
The critical point for this industry is that 800 V DC does not solve the dynamic load problem on its own. NVIDIA has been explicit that energy storage is required alongside it to stabilize supply against load fluctuation.
Removing conversion stages also removes the buffering those stages incidentally provided. Something has to absorb the transients, and in the new topology that something is a battery on the DC bus at facility scale, at the rack, or both.
This raises the bar considerably. A cell entering a 1 MW HVDC rack must deliver high C-rate discharge, high volumetric energy density in a severely constrained envelope, long calendar and cycle life at elevated temperature, and a voltage window compatible with high-efficiency DC/DC conversion.
That last criterion is where several promising chemistries struggle. Sodium-ion's wider full-cell operating voltage range, driven largely by the sloped profile of hard carbon anodes, forces more complex buck/boost conversion in DC UPS duty. This is a real penalty in an architecture whose entire premise is fewer conversion stages.
For battery manufacturers and data center operators, these shifts create both challenges and opportunities. Four strategic considerations stand out:
Strategic recommendations for battery procurement
1. Specify for the rack after next
A battery qualified for a 100 kW rack in a 415 V AC hall may have no path into a 1 MW HVDC rack. Future-proofing means designing to the DC bus voltage window, the C-rate, and the volumetric envelope of the architecture that is arriving, not the one being retired.
Qualification cycles for critical power infrastructure are long enough that anything else is a one-generation product.
2. Treat architecture simplification as the product requirement
Every conversion stage eliminated is efficiency, capital cost, and floor area recovered. Chemistries that force an additional DC/DC stage work against the value proposition they are being sold into.
Storage native to the DC bus captures value that storage bolted onto it does not.
Credit: Mohammadi, et al, Grid Integration of AI Data Centers: A Critical Review of Energy Storage Solutions (CC-BY-4.0)
3. Price white space correctly
As siting, zoning, and permitting get harder, footprint stops being fungible. Every square foot of grey space consumed by battery rooms, UPS gear, and conversion equipment is white space that cannot host revenue-generating compute.
Energy and power density are not engineering vanity metrics here; they convert directly into deployable IT capacity on a constrained parcel.
4. Look at high-performance cells that collapse two systems into one
The conventional assumption is that power quality and critical power need separate solutions: high-rate cells or supercapacitors for transients, a separate energy-optimized string for ride-through. Silicon anode cells may challenge that.
Amprius Technologies has commercialized cells reaching up to 450 Wh/kg and 1,150 Wh/L with discharge rates up to 10C. A cell delivering both extreme power and extreme energy density can, in an online double-conversion UPS configuration, smooth GPU transients and carry ride-through duty from the same asset in a fraction of the volume, with one BMS (Battery Management System), one thermal system, and one qualification pathway.
Credit: Ratel Consulting
The window is closing
The AI data center is the first market at gigawatt scale where power, response time, controllability, and density outrank cost per kilowatt-hour. Lead-acid held the critical power franchise for decades because the job never changed.
The job has now changed.
As hyperscalers race to deploy gigawatt-scale AI campuses and rack densities push past 1 MW, the battery technologies that win this market will be those that treat power architecture as product specification. The window to qualify for the next generation is closing.

is the principal consultant & founder of Ratel Consulting LLC. Ratel is a boutique management consultancy focused on growth through innovation to create value for clients with every engagement. Battery technology is a core practice area at Ratel. Charlie’s experience with
robotics, drones, AI data centers, and EVs
catalyzes growth and simplifies navigation for clients in rapidly evolving business and technical domains.

title: BYD Expands Globally with Innovations in Battery Technology
content:
Charging
EV Batteries
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Automotive & Mobility
Explore how BYD transforms the EV industry with FLASH charging technology, offering charging capping at 97% SOC and robust battery warranties.
September 1, 2026
3 Min Read
BYD FLASH charging station.
Courtesy of BYD.
BYD, short for "Build Your Dreams," has ambitious global expansion plans in the electric vehicle (EV) industry. In the second quarter of 2026, the company reported a 30% increase in profit—its first quarterly profit rise in over a year. While this growth fell short of
analysts' 48% expectations
, it underscores BYD's resilience in a competitive landscape.
Reuters stated, "The world's largest EV maker by shipments has been at the forefront of Chinese automakers' overseas push, gaining market share across Europe and Southeast Asia..." This diversification reflects BYD's commitment to reducing its reliance on an increasingly crowded domestic market while solidifying its leadership in the global EV sector.
According to
Nikkei Asia
, BYD is also leveraging its X-PACK technology—first introduced in Japan—in Europe to develop small EVs. The space-saving LFP battery pack (35.84 kWh) that powers the compact Racco EV will be repurposed to build affordable, efficient EVs for Europe.
Related:
Schneider Electric Launches Home EV Charger That Works With Existing Electrical Systems
BYD Racco. Courtesy of BYD Japan media center.
BYD's Blade battery and FLASH charging technology
In March 2026, BYD unveiled two technologies to address some of the most persistent challenges in the EV industry: slow charging speeds and poor low-temperature charging performance. The company announced the 2nd Generation Blade battery (one of the
fastest-charging EV batteries
in 2026) and FLASH charging technology.
The latest technology allows EVs to charge from 10% to 70% State of Charge (SOC) in just 5 minutes and reach 97% SOC in only 9 minutes. And according to BYD, even at extremely low temperatures, such as -30°C, the charging time from 20% to 97% increases by only 3 minutes compared to room temperature. These advancements address range anxiety and critical concerns about charging reliability in diverse climates.
BYD announced 20,000 FLASH charging stations across China, and it has initiated a large-scale global rollout by the end of 2026. According to
Car News China
, the company recently reached its 10,000th FLASH Charging Station in Shenzhen, marking the halfway point toward its full-year target and further solidifying its leadership in ultra-fast charging technology.
View post on X
Why BYD caps FLASH charging speeds at 97% SOC
One intriguing aspect for prospective users of BYD's FLASH charging technology is its decision to cap charging speeds at 97% SOC rather than 100%. Charging a battery to 100% SOC involves a process known as "trickle charging," which is significantly slower and less efficient than charging up to 97%.
The final few percentage points require a gradual reduction in charging power to prevent overheating and ensure safety. In other words, the final 3% of charging is like filling a glass to the brim—it requires extra care to avoid spillage. Moreover, fast-charging to 100% SOC can accelerate battery degradation over time, as it places additional stress on the cells. Pushing a massive amount of electrical current—up to 1,500 kW—into the last 3% of a battery pack generates severe heat and chemical stress.

title: Why RFID Success in RTI Programmes Starts With the Label

Why RFID Success in RTI Programmes Starts With the Label
Prioritise Us
on Google
RFID is transforming supply chains by increasing visibility and reliability. Credit: Checkpoint
As supply chains become more automated and sustainability targets become more ambitious, reusable assets are playing a bigger role in day-to-day operations
Returnable transport items (RTIs) such as pallets, crates, totes and reusable containers help reduce waste, lower packaging costs and support circular supply chain initiatives.
As a result, more businesses are replacing single-use packaging with reusable assets that circulate continuously across suppliers, manufacturing sites, distribution centres and customers.
But greater reuse brings greater complexity.
RFID-Enabled Circularity. Credit: Checkpoint
Tackling an issue
Unlike disposable packaging, RTIs are valuable operational assets. They spend their lives moving through multiple facilities, transport partners and washing cycles before returning to service again. Without reliable visibility, assets can be misplaced, left idle, lost or replaced unnecessarily. Even small visibility gaps can create supply chain disruptions, operational inefficiencies and additional costs.
That's why more supply chain leaders are investing in technologies that provide accurate, real-time asset visibility. RFID has become one of the most effective ways to identify, track and manage reusable assets at scale, helping teams understand where assets are, how they are being used and when they are ready for redeployment.
Checkpoint label. Credit: Checkpoint
But successful RFID programmes depend on more than readers and software. It starts with the label.
RTI environments are demanding. Assets are exposed to repeated handling, moisture, industrial washing processes, temperature changes and constant movement throughout the supply chain. These conditions can quickly affect labels that were not designed for long-term reusable asset applications.
When labels fail, read performance suffers. When read performance suffers, visibility becomes harder to trust.
That's why
choosing the right RFID label
is such an important part of any reusable asset programme.
Here at Checkpoint, we’ve developed RFID labels specifically for reusable assets and RTI applications. They’re engineered to maintain reliable performance throughout repeated use cycles, helping you keep assets identifiable and visible for longer, even in demanding supply chain environments.
Checkpoint's labels help increase visibility. Credit: Checkpoint
Whether you’re tracking reusable crates in fresh food supply chains, containers in automotive manufacturing or totes moving through distribution networks, reliable reads support better operational decisions at every stage of the asset lifecycle.
You can reduce manual tracking.
You can improve inventory accuracy.
You can identify losses more quickly.
And you can make better use of the assets already in your network.
The label may be a small part of an RFID deployment, but it has a direct impact on the quality of the data you receive. Consistent reads create more reliable information. More reliable information creates greater operational confidence.
That’s why durability matters just as much as performance.
Every successful RFID programme relies on thousands of successful reads. And every successful read starts with a label built for the realities of the supply chain.
Planning an RFID programme for reusable assets? The right label can make all the difference.

title: Zero will soon add the main feature its electric motorcycles have always lacked
content:
Zero Motorcycles just announced that coming in 2027 is a much requested feature that the company has yet to include on its electric motorcycles: DC fast charging.
Details are still extremely thin. Before leaving its home in the US last year, the company lost much of its management team, and layoffs included its PR and Communications departments. The ripple effects are still being felt with these kinds of big announcements now being made on social media with little opportunity for follow-ups or extra detail.
But what we can glean is that the company seems set on adding the one feature its electric motorcycles have long gone without: the fastest charging technology.
Zero hasn’t yet said exactly which models will receive the new charging technology other than some street and dual-sport models, what charging standard it will use, or what kind of peak charging power riders can expect, but did confirm that some models from as far back as the 2022 model year may be able to upgrade to DC fast charging technology that will roll out on new models next year.
For years, Zero has leaned solely on AC charging. Its current higher-end motorcycles can charge surprisingly quickly by Level 2 standards. The SR/F, for example, comes with a 6.6 kW onboard charger and can be upgraded to 12.6 kW with an additional Rapid Charging Module, giving a nearly full recharge in around 90 minutes when paying for the higher power and bulkier charger module.
But that’s still AC charging, requiring the motorcycle to carry the heavy hardware necessary to convert AC power into DC power for the battery.
DC fast charging, on the other hand, bypasses the extra step of converting the electricity on the bike, instead allowing the dedicated charging station to dump higher power directly into the battery itself.
Zero’s own website currently lists Level 3 DC fast charging as “not yet available for Zero Motorcycles,” and even describes it as a less convenient charging option due to the fewer number of stations compared to slower Level 2 chargers, going as far as to say that “stations are hard to find.” But the lack of DC fast charging has become an increasingly conspicuous omission as electric motorcycles have matured and other major brands long ago adopted the rapid charging standard for some of their electric motorcycles.
Top comment by Greyvagabond
There may be "more" Level 2 chargers in the world, but there are absolutely more DC fast chargers on normal highway routes and rest stops. In fact, I almost never see Level 2 chargers at rest stops.
Furthermore, being "able" to charge at 12.6 kW on a Level 2 charger is completely worthless; I have been driving EVs since 2015 and have never seen a Level 2 charger in the wild that charged at more than 7.2 kW, and even then its usually 6.6 kW shared (so 3.3 kW if there's a car charging next to you).
Being able to throw the bike on an easily-accessed DC fast charger off a highway is a HUGE capability boost, even if the charging rate is probably going to be very "slow" given the small battery. I'd be shocked if it even hit 50kW as a max. But this makes taking the bike on a longer highway trip possible; usually, if you wanted to ride one of these up in the mountains, you'd have to trailer it to your cabin/hotel first. But if you have the patience, you can just ride it up now and have a leisurely lunch/snack during the charging breaks.
DC fast charging can make a major difference for longer-distance riding, allowing riders to add significant range during a relatively short stop instead of planning trips around longer Level 2 charging sessions. It’s how many long-distance electric motorcycle records have been set and how e-motorcycle riders can engage in cross-country touring rides long performed by more primitive combustion-engine motorcycles.
And when it comes to the benefits of DC fast charging, electric motorcycles arguably stand to benefit even more than electric cars. With much smaller batteries than electric cars, an electric motorcycle doesn’t necessarily need enormous triple-digit charging power to dramatically reduce charging stops.
There are still plenty of unanswered questions, especially whether Zero’s 2027 DC fast charging solution will require new battery architecture, whether it will be limited to specific models, or whether there will be an upcharge as with for the higher power AC charging options the company currently offers.
But after years of Zero riders asking when DC fast charging would finally arrive, we now have an answer: 2027.

Range Rover Electric
Peter Johnson
| Sep 2 2026 - 7:45 am PT
Range Rover Electric
is now on sale with prices starting at about $140,000. It’s expensive, but the electric SUV is “the most accomplished Range Rover ever,” offering a quieter, more refined drive.
Range Rover Electric SUV prices and range
It’s finally here. After opening the waiting list in late 2023, Range Rover’s first EV received
over 61,000
interested clients.
Now, buyers can finally place an order. JLR opened orders for the Range Rover Electric on Wednesday, starting at $140,450 for the base SE trim.
The electric SUV is unmistakably still a Range Rover, retaining the British automaker’s iconic reductive design. As an EV, it does feature a few slight differences, such as a closed-off grille, new wheels, and a tailored underbody to optimize range and efficiency.
According to Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, the electric SUV underwent the most intensive testing of any of its vehicles to date to ensure it is “genuinely the most accomplished Range Rover ever.”
The electric propulsion takes the luxury SUV to the next level as the quietest, most responsive Range Rover yet.
Range Rover Electric towing (Source: JLR)
Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, the setup delivers “V8 levels of power” with a combined 542 horsepower and 627 lb-ft of torque. The setup enables it to accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in as little as 4.3 seconds.
Range Rover’s electric SUV uses an “industry-leading” 118.5 kWh lithium-ion double-stack battery with 344 prismatic cells, providing an EPA-estimated 333 miles of driving range. Under WLTP conditions, it offers up to 372 miles.
Based on an 800V electric architecture, the Range Rover Electric’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes. It can also add about 136 miles of range in 10 minutes of charging.
In North America, all versions have a built-in NACS port so that drivers can access Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. In the UK and Europe, JLR said drivers will have access to over one million public chargers.
New tech, developed exclusively for the electric SUV, enables it to outperform the gas version in most areas.
For example, the new Intelligent Driveline Dynamics (IDD) and Integrated Traction Management (ITM) controls motor speed within 50 milliseconds and manages slip up to 100 times quicker than an equivalent ICE vehicle.
JLR said the Range Rover Electric can wade through up to 35.4″ (900 mm) of water, on par with the gas version.
Range Rover also introduced a new app that allows drivers to manage climate functions, check the battery level, and schedule charging when the vehicle is plugged in.
Orders are now open for the Range Rover Electric, starting at $140,450 in the US and £154,070 in the UK, OTR.
It’s available in standard and long wheelbase variants. The standard Range Rover Electric measures 199″ long, 81″ wide, and 74″ tall with a 118″ wheelbase. The LWB model, on the other hand, is 207″ long, 81″ wide, and 74″ tall with a 126″ wheelbase.
The Range Rover Electric LWB First Edition starts at $183,850 and adds a front center console fridge, Tailgate Event Suite package, and illuminated metal treadplates with First Edition badges.

title: Polestar 4 SUV launches at €57,900 — and it finally has a rear window
content:
Fred Lambert
| Sep 2 2026 - 7:39 am PT
The Polestar 4 SUV. Source: Polestar
Polestar launched the Polestar 4 SUV today, a new body style of its compact executive electric SUV that starts at €57,900 and delivers up to 630 km of WLTP range.
The bigger news for anyone who followed the original car: unlike the Polestar 4 coupé, the SUV has an actual rear window.
The rear window returns
When Polestar unveiled the Polestar 4 in 2023, the headline feature was a missing one. The coupé shipped
with no rear window at all
, replacing it with a roof-mounted camera feeding a digital rear-view mirror. Polestar argued the design freed up rear headroom and enabled a larger panoramic roof, but it became the car’s most divisive talking point.
Unlike the Polestar 4 coupé, the SUV has a rear window. Source: Polestar
The Polestar 4 SUV reverses that call. Polestar says the new variant “opens the rear vision-field towards the tailgate with a rear window” and comes with a conventional rear-view mirror as standard. Customers who preferred the camera setup can still option the digital rear-view mirror that launched on the coupé.
It’s a rare, quiet acknowledgment that the original bet didn’t land with everyone — and it comes wrapped in a more practical package.
More space, same platform
The Polestar 4 SUV is built on the same Geely SEA architecture as the
, but a straighter roofline and more upright tailgate open up the back.
The Polestar 4 SUV offers up to 1,665 litres of cargo space. Source: Polestar
The SUV offers 1,680 liters of total storage across front and rear compartments, expanding to 1,665 liters of luggage capacity with the rear seats folded. The taller rear end adds 2.5 centimeters of second-row headroom over the already-roomy coupé, and full-length roof rails raise dynamic roof load capacity to 100 kg.
A larger standard panoramic glass roof stretches to the tailgate, with an optional electrochromic version — unique to the SUV — that lets occupants dim the glass through the center display.
Two powertrains, 100 kWh standard
Every Polestar 4 SUV gets a 100 kWh battery. The rear motor version pairs 200 kW (272 hp) with up to 630 km of WLTP range and a 0-100 km/h time of 7.3 seconds. The dual motor all-wheel-drive version delivers 400 kW (544 hp) and 686 Nm, dropping the 0-100 km/h sprint to 3.9 seconds while offering up to 600 km of range.
The Polestar 4 SUV interior, now with Google Gemini. Source: Polestar
Charging tops out at 200 kW DC and 22 kW AC in selected markets. A Performance pack adds ZF active dampers, Brembo brakes with gold calipers, and 22-inch wheels on Pirelli P Zero tires.
Polestar also confirmed Vehicle-to-Load is coming to all Polestar 4 vehicles, delivering up to 3.3 kW of AC power through a certified adapter, alongside a new Camping mode that turns the parked car into a climate-controlled space. Google Gemini replaces Google Assistant as the in-car voice AI, rolling out across 22 countries in 16 languages.
Pricing and availability
Polestar 4 SUV pricing starts at €57,900 for the Rear motor, €65,900 for the Dual motor, and €76,300 for the Performance pack (German base prices, incl. VAT).
The SUV is built in Busan, South Korea, where production started in the second quarter of 2026. First customer deliveries are planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. Polestar CEO Michael Lohscheller said the first shipment “is on the way to our customers.”
Electrek’s Take
Personally, I didn’t have any problem with the lack of a rear window in the Polestar 4. It was better implemented than in the Cybertruck, for example. But this is still the right move. The company took its best-selling model, gave it the practicality buyers actually want — more cargo, more headroom, roof rails, V2L, a camping mode — and quietly fixed the one feature everyone complained about.
The timing matters. Polestar just posted
record retail sales of 30,423 cars in the first half of 2026
, but it’s still deeply unprofitable and leaning on Geely for support. A more versatile, better-priced version of its most successful model is exactly the kind of low-risk volume play it needs right now, and €57,900 in Germany undercuts a lot of the compact executive SUV field on paper.
Of course, this version of the vehicle could do well in the US and since it is being produced in South Korea rather than China, it looks like Polestar was aiming for the US market – a decision it likely made before
being kicked out of the market
I think Polestar makes great EVs that are really fun to drive. I hope Geely keeps supporting them because I truly believe that they could become an impressive brand if they can find their footing in this currently wild EV market, especially for them in the US.

title: Republicans are about to raise your fuel costs by 45% during an energy crisis
content:
fuel economy
Department of Transportation
Reality TV
Jameson Dow
| Sep 2 2026 - 7:00 am PT
Former reality TV contestant Sean Duffy.
The Department of Transportation says it’s ready to announce fuel economy standards that will raise average fuel costs by 45%, right as the world struggles with the effects of a war of choice that has
spiked energy prices globally
Since the 1970s, the US government has had various rules that guide auto manufacturers to make and sell more efficient vehicles.
The main standards, Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE), were first implemented after the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s, and the ensuing energy crisis. The standards require manufacturers to maintain an average level of fuel efficiency across their fleet, or else they have to pay a fine for every noncompliant car they sell.
Prior to these standards, American cars were large and gas guzzling, with very little interest in efficiency. CAFE standards and other government regulations related to efficiency and clean air, both on the state and federal level, have made cars cleaner and more efficient as time has gone on.
The result of cleaner and more efficient vehicles is that it costs less to fuel them, costs less to breathe the dirty air they cause, and makes the environment that you depend on for everything good in your life more livable.
So, of course, republicans want to end all of that.
DoT ‘about to announce’ effort to raise your fuel costs
This week, Sean Duffy, the
former reality TV contestant posing as the current head of the Department of Transportation said that he is “about to announce” new fuel economy standards that stand to increase average American fuel costs dramatically.
These fuel economy standards aren’t a surprise – on his
very first day
, Duffy signed a memo promising to increase US fuel costs, reversing standards that were estimated to save Americans $23 billion. But his intent was to target
fuel economy standard whatsoever, wanting to eliminate anything that saves you money, as $23 billion wasn’t enough for him.
Over time, that intent has been refined and
officially proposed
as a reduction in 2031 target average fuel economy from 50.4mpg to 34.5mpg. The NHTSA says that in fact, these changes would raise fuel costs by $185 billion, and carbon emissions by 5%. These numbers do not take into account the higher health costs from more pollution (but the White House
literally says your life is worth nothing
, anyway).
Then it was
put up for public comment
, and the vast majority of the
68,294 comments
naturally opposed the plan to hike your fuel and health costs and make the environment less livable.
The changes could raise fuel costs by more than 45%
Doing some simple math, lowering fuel economy from 50.4 mpg to 34.5 mpg would raise the average fuel required to go the same distance by 45% – meaning that average total fuel costs will go up by
at least
45% if cars meet the new standards rather than the old ones.
Why “at least” 45%? Well, not only would this regulation mean that drivers have to buy more gasoline on average, but it also means that gasoline prices would go up even further as demand goes up.
You need look no further than
an analysis released by the Department of Energy
which said that gas prices will go up by 76 cents per gallon if republicans’ energy plans were to take effect. And before anyone claims partisanship – this report was signed off on by Chris Wright, the oil CEO
currently squatting in the DoE (who of course sees higher gas prices as a good thing, since it makes more money for his industry).

title: Tesla settles fatal Autopilot fire truck lawsuit, avoiding jury trial
content:
Fred Lambert
| Sep 2 2026 - 6:37 am PT
Tesla has settled a wrongful death lawsuit over a 2023 crash in which a Model S on Autopilot slammed into a parked fire truck, killing the driver and seriously injuring his brother.
The confidential settlement, filed in California federal court, lets Tesla avoid a jury trial that would have put Elon Musk’s own Autopilot claims in front of jurors.
A Model S on Autopilot at 70 mph
The crash happened on February 18, 2023, at around 4 a.m. on Interstate 680 in Contra Costa County, California. Genesis Giovanni Mendoza Martinez, 31, was driving his 2014 Tesla Model S with Autopilot engaged when the car plowed into a county ladder fire truck parked across lanes at an earlier accident scene.
The Model S was traveling roughly 70 mph. Mendoza was killed. His brother, Caleb Mendoza, was in the passenger seat and was seriously injured.
The case,
Caleb Mendoza et al. v. Tesla, Inc.
(No. 24-cv-08738-VC), was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California before Judge Vince Chhabria. The plaintiffs were represented by Singleton Schreiber — the same firm behind a growing docket of fatal Autopilot cases against Tesla.
The claim Tesla didn’t want in front of a jury
The lawsuit didn’t rest only on a product defect theory. It alleged that Tesla and Musk misrepresented what Autopilot could actually do, leading Mendoza to over-trust a Level 2 driver-assistance system marketed with a name that implies far more.
In a May 2025 ruling, Judge Chhabria let that argument stand. He dismissed the plaintiffs’ concealment claim but allowed the fraudulent misrepresentation claims to proceed, finding the “Autopilot” name itself “plausibly misleading” — and ruling that Musk’s public statements, including that Autopilot was “probably better” than a human driver, were legally actionable.
That ruling set up a trial in which Musk’s years of autonomy promises would become evidence. Instead, Tesla settled. The terms were not disclosed.
Tesla keeps buying its way out of a verdict
The settlement fits a now-familiar pattern: Tesla resolves its fatal Autopilot and Full Self-Driving cases quietly, right before they reach a jury.
The one time it didn’t, it lost badly. A Florida federal jury hit Tesla with a
historic $243 million verdict
in a 2019 Autopilot death, and the judge refused to throw it out in February. Since then, Tesla has moved to settle case after case, including a
fatal Full Self-Driving pedestrian crash
in June.
The pressure is only building. Tesla is now
facing up to $14.5 billion in Autopilot and FSD lawsuits
, and the plaintiffs’ bar has been
emboldened by the Florida win
What makes these cases hard to litigate in the open is Tesla’s data. As we detailed in our investigation,
Tesla hides the fatal Autopilot and FSD crashes buried in its federal safety reports
— redacting crash narratives on 99.9% of its filings every year since 2019, while automakers like GM, Ford, and Toyota redact almost none.
Electrek’s Take
Every one of these confidential settlements is a data point, and the data points all say the same thing: Tesla does not want a jury weighing Musk’s autonomy claims against a dead driver.
Tesla might have convinced its shareholders that it solved autonomy, but that claim is simply not standing in court, and Tesla knows it.
The Mendoza case was especially dangerous because Judge Chhabria had already ruled that “Autopilot” is plausibly misleading and that Musk’s statements are fair game. That’s the crux of the entire liability theory — that Tesla built a Level 2 system, named it something that implies autonomy, and let its CEO narrate it as effectively self-driving for a decade. A trial would have forced that argument into the open with discovery, telemetry, and Musk’s own words. Settling makes it disappear.
The confidentiality is the point. Tesla pays to keep the number secret and the evidence sealed, so no single case becomes the precedent that opens the floodgates any wider than the $243 million Florida verdict already has. It’s a rational legal strategy, but it’s also an admission: when Tesla can’t get these cases dismissed, it doesn’t fight them in front of a jury — it pays to make them go away.
The question is how long that math holds as the lawsuit count climbs and the redacted crash reports keep piling up.

title: Tesla's new Model Y L is experiencing suspension failures
content:
Tesla Model YL
Jameson Dow
| Sep 2 2026 - 6:00 am PT
Several Chinese owners of Tesla’s new
Model Y L
, the larger 3-row version of the popular Model Y, are going to Chinese social media to complain about suspension collapse issues – and it’s enough of a problem that fans have developed a “finger method” to test whether a vehicle is affected.
Tesla released the Model Y L in China
almost exactly one year ago
, and the model got
okay reviews
in the brutally competitive Chinese Ev market. It had several improvements over the standard Model Y at the time, and a larger wheel base which allowed for a third row of seats – though those rear seats could only be occupied by rather small people.
The model did debut to an impressive wave of sales, but over the longer term, Tesla sales in China have
continued to fall
– though perhaps less than the sales of other foreign brands that are getting absolutely crushed by domestic electric vehicle competition.
Now, Tesla seems to be seeing a new set of problems, at least according to Chinese social media reports.
The issue was recently covered on
CarNewsChina
, but the first collection of reports seems to have been posted in early August on
, a Chinese product review/recommendation site (the name seems to be Chinese shorthand for “What’s Worth Buying”).
The report says that in the period of June through August, Chinese social media had seen a pattern of complaints of rear suspension collapse on the new longer, heavier vehicles. The complaints were sourced from Xiaohongshu, sometimes referred to in the West as “Chinese Instagram.”
Users posted various photos of Model Y L vehicles with low rear wheel arches, with smzdm finding at least ten posts showing the same issue, and hundreds of comments on those posts complaining.
On those posts, owners have developed a “finger test” for other owners to follow as a simple check whether their vehicle might be affected. Simply put your hand inbetween the wheel and wheel arch: if 4 fingers fit, you’re fine; if 3 fingers fit, watch out; if fewer than 3 fingers fit, your suspension has probably been affected by this issue.
A more accurate test can be done with a measuring tape, measuring from the ground. Normal heights run from 764-804mm. If your wheel arch is less than 764mm off the ground, this will qualify for a replacement from Tesla, per its service guidelines.
A lower rear suspension can dangerously affect handling characteristics, and at the very least alters tire wear patterns to prematurely wear out tires. Some users report a feeling of “swaying” at the rear of affected vehicles.
Most of the affected vehicles seem to have come from the first batch of cars, delivered in September and October of 2025. These cars have mostly been fixed under warranty, but the issue has recurred for some of the vehicles even after service was done on them.
But users are suggesting vigilance. Since Tesla China has not yet made a statement about the issue, social media users have suggested that owners should check their suspension monthly, and keep a log of the heights – either measured with a tape or with fingers, and taking photos to keep track of it all.
This is particularly true for older vehicles from the early batches. It could be that Tesla has improved its processes since then, or it could be that the issue just hasn’t become apparent yet on newer vehicles.
So far, it seems that most vehicles are having the issue solved under warranty, but vigilance is still important. The same applies to overseas Y L owners with Shanghai-assembled cars, such as those in Australia and New Zealand, who should keep an eye on their rear suspension.
This isn’t the first time Tesla has had suspension issues. The US NHTSA is currently
probing Tesla over suspension failure
it has done before
), though those are about the front suspension, not the rear. And in Germany, the Model Y was found to have a
high defect rate
in annual testing, with suspension being the main source of issues.
Whether this same rear suspension issue will affect the US version of the Model Y L, which was just
launched in July
, is another question. Chinese models are assembled in Tesla’s Shanghai factory, and US models are assembled in Texas. There have been differences between US and Shanghai-built models in the past, so we really have no idea yet whether this problem will be present on US models. Until Tesla develops and announces a fix, keep your fingers ready.

title: Donut Lab hits 409 Wh/kg in battery lab test, but credibility is gone
content:
Donut Lab has published a new independent test claiming its battery reached an energy density of 409 Wh/kg and 805 Wh/L, the first energy-density figure the company has put on record after months of scrutiny.
But the number lands against a promise the company has already broken: that this “solid-state” cell was in production and ready to power a production EV by the end of Q1 2026. It isn’t, and it wasn’t.
The claim was never the number — it was “production ready”
When Donut Lab unveiled its battery at CES in January, the headline wasn’t 409 Wh/kg. It was readiness. The company called it “the world’s first solid state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing” and said Verge Motorcycles would be “the world’s first production vehicle to feature this breakthrough technology,” with “first deliveries in Q1 2026.”
That claim — a solid-state cell not five years out, but shipping in a real vehicle within months — is the only reason we covered it. We’ve been burned enough times by battery breakthrough announcements that never leave the lab. Donut Lab’s pitch was different specifically because it wasn’t a lab claim. It was a production claim.
We are now in September. There is no production EV running Donut Lab’s battery on the road. The company’s own internal videos, surfaced in our June investigation, showed the “production” motorcycles were pre-production units being used to refine the manufacturing process. CEO Marko Lehtimäki later admitted in Finnish media that the cell being tested “is not even the cell that’s going to be shipped to customers.”
What the new VTT test actually measured
The new report comes from VTT Technical Research Centre, Finland’s respected national lab, and it’s a legitimate measurement. VTT weighed and measured a single cell — a “Donut Battery V1.5,” designated DL6 — and discharged it across its full 2.3–4.25V range at a 0.1C rate at 25°C. Energy divided by mass gave 409.3 Wh/kg; energy divided by volume gave 804.7 Wh/L.
“This was a fairly straightforward test,” said Donut Lab CTO Ville Piippo. He’s right — measuring energy density is trivial, which is exactly why its absence from the company’s previous five VTT tests was so conspicuous.
The problem is what the number does not establish.
A high energy density is not proof of solid-state — or of anything new
409 Wh/kg is a strong figure, but it does not require solid-state chemistry, and it does not distinguish Donut Lab’s cell from advanced lithium-ion. Amprius already sells a conventional liquid-electrolyte, silicon-anode lithium-ion cell rated at 450 Wh/kg. Top commercial high-nickel cells sit around 250–300 Wh/kg, and solid-state pilots from QuantumScape, Toyota, and Samsung SDI target 350–450 Wh/kg.
In other words, 409 Wh/kg sits comfortably inside what good lithium-ion already does.
The result is also a best case. The earlier VTT capacity test discharged at 1C down to 2.7V. This one discharges 10 times slower and 0.4V deeper — both choices that maximize the extractable energy and inflate the density figure.
And it’s a different cell again. VTT’s own report describes the DL6 as “an energy-optimised variant of the V1 cell.” So the record now includes at least three cells: the V1 that was independently pegged as lithium-ion, the V1.5 that hit 409 Wh/kg, and a separate “next-generation” cell examined by Intertek. Insider Lauri Peltola, the former commercial chief of manufacturing partner Nordic Nano, alleged in an April criminal complaint that the independently tested battery was “an old generation that Donut and its partners gave up on.” Donut Lab denies wrongdoing.
Still no cycle life, and a “proof” that proves less than it claims
Six independent tests in, there is still zero data on Donut Lab’s most extraordinary claim: a design life of up to 100,000 cycles. This test ran two capacity cycles and stopped.
Donut Lab’s cleanest new argument is that Intertek confirmed a bipolar internal structure, and that “a bipolar cell structure is possible only with a solid electrolyte.” But what Intertek reportedly confirmed is the structure, series-connected layers with split metal-foil electrodes, not that the electrolyte is solid. The jump from “bipolar” to “therefore solid-state” is Donut Lab’s inference, and it’s made on a different cell than the one that hit 409 Wh/kg. If that’s hard to follow, it might be on purpose. A separate nail-penetration test showing the cell stayed stable is a real safety result, but safety is not proof of chemistry either — plenty of lithium-ion and LFP cells pass it.
VTT, for its part, makes no chemistry determination at all. The word “solid-state” appears in the report only as the customer’s project name.
Electrek’s Take
Let’s be clear about what Donut Lab actually promised, because the company keeps moving the goalpost to wherever the latest test happens to land. The promise was not “we can hit 400 Wh/kg in a lab.” The promise was a solid-state battery in a production vehicle by the end of Q1 2026. That was the whole story, and it’s the only reason a healthily skeptical EV outlet gave a battery startup the benefit of the doubt in the first place.
Top comment by ircsmith
I worked for a startup that over promised and lied to secure money. Maybe you've seen the HBO special. The CEO is in prison now and I'm glad I saw what was happening and left after only a few months. I do not understand this mindset. I would rather under promise and over deliver. Disappointed in Donut (not the cat) because of this. My plans for the next few years was to dink around with converting an ICE to BEV and use Donut motors and cells. Now I'm rethinking my plans.
That promise is now falsified — not by an investigation, but by the calendar. It’s September. There is no production EV on the road with this battery. What we have instead is a steady drip of individual lab tests, each one measuring a single cell, each one on a slightly different cell than the last, and each one carefully avoiding the two questions that actually matter: is it genuinely solid-state, and does it survive real cycling? A 409 Wh/kg number that any advanced lithium-ion maker could match does not answer either.
Our last investigation laid out in detail how Donut Lab exaggerated the readiness of its cell to reach production. These results don’t change that, they reinforce it. I’m sorry, Donut Lab, but the burden of proof has flipped. A company that promised production vehicles and delivered a press release doesn’t get to keep the benefit of the doubt. Show us the cell that ships, in the vehicle it ships in, cycling the way you claim, or stop calling it ready.

title: EU approves German capacity mechanism - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The European Commission has approved Germany’s capacity mechanism, clearing the way for up to €35.2 billion in state support for generation, storage and demand-side flexibility. The scheme will use competitive auctions and require new gas-fired power plants to be hydrogen-ready, with climate-neutral operation required by 2045.
Sandra Enkhardt
02 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
The European Commission approved, under EU state aid rules, Germany’s capacity mechanism under the StromVKG, which is due to take effect in 2031. The legislation also provides for two additional tenders this year, each covering 4.5 GW of capacity, which are expected to be awarded largely to new gas-fired power plants.
The measures are intended to secure sufficient generation, storage and demand-side flexibility to ensure reliable electricity supply. Following the Commission’s approval, the German government can allocate an estimated €15.6 billion ($18.1 billion) to €35.2 billion to support the required capacity.
The Commission said the capacity mechanism must be open to all technologies, including generation, storage and demand-side response, as well as existing and cross-border capacity. Capacity required from 2031 will be procured through competitive auctions. Contracts will run for 15 years, while participating facilities must operate on a climate-neutral basis by 2045 at the latest. New gas-fired power plants will therefore have to be capable of running on hydrogen.
The first two auctions under the StromVKG scheme are still scheduled to take place this year, with the first due to begin on Sept. 8. Further auctions for long-duration capacity are planned between 2027 and 2029.
According to the Commission, the measure is expected to cost between €1 billion and €3 billion in 2031, depending on the auction results. Annual costs from 2032 to 2045 are estimated at between €900 million and €2.3 billion.
The Commission concluded that the measures are “necessary and appropriate” and that the aid is “proportionate” to the funding required.
“Just in time for the first bid submission date – Sept. 8, 2026 – the European Commission has granted state aid approval. After three and a half years of intense negotiations, evolving drafts and repeated delays, the conditions for new dispatchable capacities have thus been established,” the Executive Director of the German Association of Energy and Water Industries, Kerstin Andreae, said following the approval.
“It is now crucial for the Federal Network Agency to quickly award the contracts so that the facilities can be implemented rapidly. The next step is to design the broad capacity market – open to all technologies – for the period starting in 2032. This should be based on the requirements outlined in the StromVKG,” Andreae added.

title: What happens to a ready-to-build solar project if a wildfire hits the site? - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
What happens if a wildfire affects a ready-to-build (RTB) solar project? Can developers recover their financial guarantees if the project becomes unviable? Jochen Beckmann, a lawyer at Rödl Barcelona, analyzes the key legal and administrative implications for
pv magazine
Pilar Sánchez Molina
02 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
A forest fire can force a review of the technical, environmental and economic conditions of a solar project, even after it has reached ready-to-build (RTB) status. In some cases, it could also make the project technically unfeasible.
While a fire does not automatically invalidate existing permits or result in project cancellation, changes to site conditions can trigger new administrative requirements and revisions to environmental and fire-protection measures. They can also affect the project’s economic viability.
Jochen Beckmann, a lawyer at Rödl Barcelona, spoke with
pv magazine
about the legal and administrative consequences a forest fire can have for an authorized solar project in Spain.
Once a project reaches RTB status, it typically holds preliminary administrative authorization (AAP), administrative construction authorization (AAC), an environmental impact statement (DIA) and the corresponding municipal building permit.
According to Beckmann, the situation can change substantially, however, if a forest fire affects part or all of the project site shortly before construction begins.
Such a scenario could arise, for example, from a lightning-induced fire. “Although the event is beyond the developer’s control, changes to the site’s physical and environmental conditions may require authorities to reassess some of the conditions underpinning the project’s existing authorizations,” the lawyer said.
Review of fire protection and safety requirements
Safety is among the first areas that may require reassessment. Authorization of a solar project is based on compliance with the technical and protection requirements applicable at the time of approval. If a fire substantially alters the surrounding environment, the relevant authorities may require a review of the project’s planned safety measures.
The review could affect the project’s self-protection plan (PAU), Beckmann stressed. A reassessment of site conditions may result in additional fire-protection requirements, such as wider vegetation-free safety buffers.
Additional buffer zones could reduce the area available for solar modules, potentially requiring changes to the project’s planned capacity.
Authorities could also require additional fire-protection infrastructure, including firefighting water reserves, hydrants or other specialized equipment. “These measures could increase project costs and affect the project’s original economic assumptions,” Beckmann added.
Updating the environmental assessment
The environmental impact statement (EIS) is based on the environmental conditions in place when the assessment is conducted. A forest fire can significantly alter those conditions and affect elements considered in the original analysis.
Potential consequences that could require reassessment include increased erosion risk, changes in vegetation, altered soil hydrology and impacts on the protection and mitigation measures established for the project.
Spain’s Law 21/2013 establishes monitoring and reporting obligations that are further defined in the conditions attached to each EIS. According to Beckmann, these statements typically require developers to notify the relevant authority of project modifications or significant events that could affect the environmental assessment, including natural events such as forest fires.
In such cases, environmental authorities may require a technical addendum to the environmental monitoring program (EMP). The document would assess changes caused by the fire and, where necessary, establish additional protection, monitoring or restoration measures.
These could include measures to prevent or reduce soil erosion, modifications to drainage and water discharge systems, measures to mitigate flooding and runoff risks during heavy rainfall, and monitoring of the recovery of affected areas.
Such changes can have implications beyond environmental compliance. “New technical requirements could affect project design, construction schedules and the cost of bringing the plant into operation,” Beckmann said.
Force majeure and financial guarantees
Another consideration is the legal classification of the fire and its potential implications for financial guarantees lodged for the project’s development.
A forest fire caused by lightning would generally meet the criteria for a force majeure event, according to Beckmann.
However, classification as force majeure does not automatically result in the return of financial guarantees. The issue becomes particularly relevant if additional technical, environmental or safety requirements imposed after the fire make the project economically unviable or technically impossible to execute.
In such cases, the developer would need to demonstrate a clear causal link between the fire and its inability to proceed with the project.
“Comprehensive documentation of the event and its specific impact on the project’s viability is decisive,” Beckmann said. The return of deposited guarantees could be considered only if the developer can sufficiently demonstrate that the fire and its consequences prevent the project from proceeding.
Documentation should therefore cover the cause and extent of the fire, as well as any resulting technical, environmental and economic changes to the project.
